title: Not a Bourbon Street band
summary: Zanco learned other keys from the band and prefers the lower register; he dislikes the modernized cymbal-and-high-note style of Bourbon Street groups.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: But you don't go for all that, uh, stuff with high notes and fast tempos?

Uh, well, no, you see, that, uh, I'll tell you something. Uh, I've always been able to play in one key only, which was B flat. Everything I played had to be played in B flat, say. But, well, since I've been playing with this group naturally, you got some, some pretty good, uh, musicians in the group. These guys really know that stuff. And over a period of a year or so, uh, I think they taught me to play in just about every, you know, every key. But, uh, I try to minimize my stuff by keeping it more on a lower scale and try to get up in the, in the atmosphere, you know. Uh, I, I, I like to play in a lower register, but, uh, it's not always effective, you know, in some tunes. So you have to get high.
Uh, but what I mean is the, the general atmosphere of the band is not that of Bourbon Street musicians.
You're not aiming for the same thing.

Well, you know, most of the bands, I don't know, maybe, maybe I shouldn't be saying this, but to me, most of the bands you're here on Bourbon Street now, uh, they all seem to get a modern trend in their music. The drummers will rely strictly on their cymbals. The trumpet players have to do these soaring notes, you know, all this high, all the high playing. And they more or less modernize it. Of course, it's still supposed to be the old tune, but they kind of modernize it, see. And, uh, I like the old jazz for what the old jazz was. See, nothing fancy. It was just, just good pure music.
